questions.subject: ANALYTICAL_CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute pH electrode potential change
questions.stem: Sample 3101: A glass pH electrode has an ideal Nernstian response of 59.16 mV per pH unit at 25 degrees Celsius. What potential change accompanies a pH change of 4.14?

options.misconception: halves the response without justification
divides the slope by the pH change instead of multiplying
ignores the magnitude of the pH change

questions.explanation: A Nernstian pH electrode changes potential linearly with pH at about fifty-nine millivolts per unit at room temperature. Multiplying by the pH change gives the total shift. Dividing or ignoring the change misuses the calibration slope.
questions.hint: Multiply millivolts per unit by the number of units.

questions.subject: ANALYTICAL_CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute Nernstian slope for an ion-selective electrode
questions.stem: Sample 3102: For an ideal ion-selective electrode at 25 degrees Celsius, what is the Nernstian slope in mV per decade for an ion of charge z = 2?

options.misconception: divides by the square of the charge
uses the monovalent slope regardless of ion charge
multiplies by charge instead of dividing by it

questions.explanation: The Nernst slope is 59.16 millivolts divided by the ionic charge for a decade change in activity. A divalent ion therefore gives roughly half the slope of a monovalent one. Multiplying by charge or ignoring it gives the wrong sensitivity.
questions.hint: Slope scales as 59.16 over z.
